title: The golden rule (Matthew 7:12)
hook: do to others what you'd want done to you

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ask, the first of ask, seek, knock. Your line was ask, and it shall be given. Did you ask someone for something plainly? Day two hundred fifty-seven.

It turns up on classroom posters, in a grandparent's advice, after a shove between siblings. Treat people the way you want to be treated. It sounds so much like common sense that it can seem to have no author at all. But it has an address. Right here, near the end of the Sermon on the Mount, one verse long, standing on its own like a signpost. And Jesus says something big about it: this one line is the law and the prophets. Today's word: golden rule.
screen: `A CLASSROOM POSTER.` → `IT HAS AN ADDRESS.` → `ONE VERSE LONG.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the King James Bible: "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets." Three things are worth noticing. First, the name. The Bible never calls it golden. That label came along much later, in English. Second, the ending: this is the law and the prophets. That was how people in Jesus's time named their scriptures, the teachings of Moses and the writings of the prophets. So he's saying: if you want the heart of the scriptures in one sentence, here it is. Third, it's phrased as something to do: what you'd love someone to do for you, go and do it first. Jesus wasn't the only teacher who found the whole of scripture in one line. The Talmud tells of the sage Hillel, who was challenged to teach the whole Torah while standing on one foot. He answered that what is hateful to you, you shouldn't do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary, now go and learn it. His version names what not to do; Jesus's names what to do. The Book of Tobit has a similar saying. Leviticus holds the root of all of them: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Christians often read the golden rule as that commandment turned into a daily test. Here's the ordinary-Tuesday version. Before you text, before you reply, before you walk past, flip the seats. If I were them right now, what would I hope for? Then do that.
screen: `NEVER CALLED GOLDEN IN THE BIBLE.` · `THE LAW AND THE PROPHETS.` · `NOT JUST AVOID: DO.` · `FLIP THE SEATS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you'd love someone to do for you this week. A text that says I'm thinking of you. A coffee left on your desk. Someone taking the trash out without being asked. Hold it for a moment. Now think of one person who might love the same thing. Picture doing it for them today. The bell holds the time.
Golden rule. Do to others what you would want done to you. The whole of the law and the prophets, in one line.
Your line: as you would be treated. Today, go and do the thing you pictured, for that one person, before the day ends. Day two hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Christian parents often teach the golden rule to children as a first rule of life, and some use it as a quick test before acting: if I were them, what would I hope for?

notes: The name 'golden rule' is usually dated to seventeenth-century English usage; the script says only 'much later, in English'. Confirm.
Hillel's saying (Shabbat 31a) is paraphrased; 'a generation or so earlier' is approximate. Confirm the dating and the respectful framing.
Tobit is scripture for Catholics and Orthodox and apocrypha for most Protestants; the script calls it 'the Book of Tobit' without ranking.

Editor review 2026-10-01: SERIOUS fix: 'this one line holds the whole Bible' overstated Matthew 7:12 (the law and the prophets); the 'it's active, not avoid hurting' point placed right before Hillel's negative form read as ranking Jesus over Hillel, now stated side by side without ranking. Also cut 'most famous sentence in the world', 'most precious rule', 'always', the Hillel dating, and the hook that told the listener when they learned it.
